assessment.nobel_worthiness: Methods for estimating demand and supply in differentiated-product markets (BLP) and dynamic oligopoly (Ericson-Pakes) changed empirical industrial organisation. They are now the standard tools for merger review, antitrust analysis and welfare measurement, and they are used well beyond IO. The contribution is both a methodological advance and a widely adopted practical toolkit.
assessment.attribution: Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes are the clearest core of the demand-estimation framework. Pakes is also central to the dynamic-industry models. Bresnahan, Benkard, Reiss and Levin made important adjacent contributions, but the three-person limit points to the BLP trio.
assessment.maturity: The core papers date from the mid-1990s and have been confirmed by about three decades of use across fields and by regulatory practice. The work is fully mature, and no timing concerns arise.
uncertainties: Bresnahan's early role in new empirical IO, and Pakes's dynamic-model work with coauthors, could shift the preferred trio.
I rely on background knowledge and have not independently verified citation or adoption counts.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Firm heterogeneity and selection into exporting transformed trade theory and empirics. It moved the field beyond representative-firm models and introduced new channels for gains from trade, with a large effect on trade policy analysis and a large body of empirical work.
assessment.attribution: Melitz (2003) is the pivotal contribution. Helpman's work on heterogeneous firms, FDI and later extensions, and on trade and politics, fits the same theme. Redding is a major contributor but more recent, and the credit is likely best split between Melitz and Helpman.
assessment.maturity: Over two decades of confirmation across theory, structural quantitative work and microdata. The field is established and the prize area is not recently covered, although Krugman received the 2008 prize for trade and location.
uncertainties: Competing claims from other heterogeneous-firm contributors such as Bernard, Eaton and Kortum, who are not on this ballot entry.
Helpman has other candidacies on the longlist (B021), which could complicate the allocation of credit.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Combines theory-grounded measurement of adverse selection and moral hazard with credible empirical designs, including the Oregon Health Insurance Experiment. The work shows how selection shapes welfare in insurance markets and has influenced health and social-insurance policy.
assessment.attribution: Finkelstein and Einav are the leading figures in empirical measurement of selection and welfare in insurance. Salanie contributed to the contract-theory and empirical-identification side. The theoretical foundations of adverse selection were already recognised in the 2001 prize.
assessment.maturity: A mature literature since the mid-2000s, with robust replication and policy use. Finkelstein's work spans more than two decades.
uncertainties: The marginal contribution relative to the earlier information-economics prize is a judgement call.
Credit among Einav, Finkelstein, Salanie and others such as Chiappori and Hendren is uncertain.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Kiyotaki-Moore credit cycles and the financial accelerator explain how collateral constraints amplify and propagate shocks. They became a core part of modern macroeconomics and the post-2008 policy debate on financial frictions.
assessment.attribution: Kiyotaki and Moore are the founders of the collateral-constraint cycle mechanism. Gertler is central to the financial accelerator and its later macro-finance development. Bernanke, who shares the accelerator work, has already been recognised (2022), which complicates the ballot entry and favours this trio.
assessment.maturity: The foundational papers date from 1989 to 1999 and have been confirmed by two decades of macro-finance work and crisis-era relevance.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises may count against the case.
Whether Gertler or Gilchrist should be credited alongside Kiyotaki and Moore.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The task-based view of technology, skill-biased change and the China trade shock reshaped understanding of wage inequality and local labour-market adjustment. The work has had a major effect on both academic work and public policy debates.
assessment.attribution: Autor is central to both the task framework and the trade-shock work. Hanson is the co-author on the China shock with Autor and Dorn. Katz has a long-standing role in the relative-demand and skill-premium literature. Dorn is also strongly tied to the China shock, so the three-person limit forces a hard choice.
assessment.maturity: The tasks work dates from about 2003 and the China-shock papers from 2013 onward. Some findings are still debated, but the main empirical patterns are well confirmed.
uncertainties: The 2021 and 2024 prizes covered labour economics and institutions, which may affect timing.
Whether the China-shock results are robust over the long run is still debated.
Dorn and Acemoglu-style task models raise attribution questions.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The alternating-offers bargaining model (1982) gave a tractable noncooperative foundation for bargaining and is a standard building block across economics, from labour markets to political economy. It also links to market-based bargaining models.
assessment.attribution: Rubinstein is the clear originator. Binmore and Wolinsky made notable related contributions, but the central result is Rubinstein's. A single-laureate proposal is the cleanest attribution.
assessment.maturity: More than 40 years of confirmation. This is a very mature contribution, and the question is whether the Committee considers it still to be unrecognised core theory.
uncertainties: Rubinstein's work on bounded rationality and other topics might support a broader citation.
Whether the Committee would regard the bargaining contribution as sufficiently distinct from existing game-theory prizes.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: A systematic theoretical and empirical framework linking electoral rules, constitutions, state capacity and fiscal outcomes. It established modern political economics and influenced work on institutions and development.
assessment.attribution: Persson and Tabellini are the main architects through their joint book and papers. Besley has a close, major role in state capacity and accountability work. The joint attribution is natural, although the three-person limit excludes other contributors.
assessment.maturity: Very mature, with 30 years of cumulative work. The 2024 prize on institutions and prosperity partially overlaps, which could count against it.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2024 prize may reduce the margin of novelty.
Persson is Swedish and has past ties to the Committee system. Under this protocol that is disclosed, not adjudicated.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Resource misallocation across firms offered a quantitative account of cross-country TFP differences and has framed much growth and development policy research. The approach is tractable and widely applied.
assessment.attribution: Hsieh and Klenow (2009) are the central authors. Restuccia and Rogerson developed closely related ideas, and the three-person limit leaves open whether to include Restuccia. The proposal names the two most identified with the empirical approach.
assessment.maturity: The measurement approach is about 15 years old and widely used. It is less time-tested than the older candidates, and the identification of misallocation from dispersion in marginal products is debated.
uncertainties: Measurement error and the interpretation of dispersion in marginal products are contested.
Priority between Restuccia-Rogerson and Hsieh-Klenow is a real attribution risk.
